title: Who's Got It Better Than Us?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. uses Jim Harbaugh's family mantra "Who's got it better than us?" to argue that cognitive science backs up an old-fashioned truth: learning requires sustained, effortful attention, and there is no way around the discomfort that entails. He walks through the basic memory pipeline (attention, working memory, long-term memory) to show why "learning is hard" is a fact of neuroscience rather than a slogan, then pivots to the psychological problem this creates: students who believe discomfort signals something has gone wrong will resist the very friction that produces growth. Stuart argues that reframing devices like Harbaugh's mantra, when repeated with "loving relentlessness," can move deeply entrenched beliefs even though they can feel silly in the moment. The piece closes by tying the practice back to real outcomes, from championship teams to a kid grinding through a math problem.
points: Learning happens only when attention, working memory, and long-term memory processing all occur — treating "learning is hard" as a memory-science fact, not classroom mythology, changes how a teacher justifies rigor to students.

Stuart identifies the core obstacle to student effort as a belief clash: when a student assumes discomfort means something is wrong, that belief — not the actual difficulty — determines whether they persist.
Repetitive, low-tech reframing devices (a mantra, a poster) can shift deeply held beliefs about difficulty when used with sustained "loving relentlessness," not as one-off pep talks.
Borrowing Jim Harbaugh's family question "Who's got it better than us?" reframes hardship as privilege rather than injustice, giving teachers a portable script for normalizing struggle.
quotes: For school stuff to go from outside of us, through the funnel of attention, through the scarce resource of working memory, and into long-term memory, work is required.
A big problem with expecting your students to do hard things in school is that…well, they're hard. They involve stress, pressure, difficulty, uncertainty.

And when that discomfort meets a student who firmly believes that discomfort is to be avoided, that when discomfort is present, something is wrong in the world — well, then you've got a clash between BELIEF and CIRCUMSTANCE.
But the thing is, these things aren't silly. When done repetitively, they begin to move that most unmovable of human forces: belief.

When done with enough loving relentlessness, these things create outcomes that seem impossible at the outset — things like winning a national championship or just working at your math problems with attention, care, and effort.
